nodes.content: Infer spatial conductivity and unknown boundary flux from sparse temperature observations while preserving uncertainty under nonidentifiability.
requirements: Achieve 90% interval coverage within five percentage points for conductivity and flux across identifiability regimes.
Match known-flux conductivity reconstruction error within 20% when joint recovery is identifiable.

nodes.content: Use hierarchical Bayesian heat-equation inversion with Gaussian-process log-conductivity, spline boundary flux, and joint MCMC posterior intervals.
How can joint posterior inference maintain calibrated conductivity and flux intervals when sparse observations leave their sensitivities nearly collinear?
Marginalizing GP and flux-spline hyperparameters yields 85–95% coverage of 90% pointwise intervals across sensitivity-matrix condition numbers 10–1000.
Simulate heat fields across condition numbers 10–1000; compare hyperparameter-marginalized MCMC coverage and identifiable-case conductivity error against known-flux inversion.
Run 200 synthetic heat-equation trials per condition-number bin (10–1000), measuring conductivity/flux interval coverage and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Across condition numbers 10–1000, 90% intervals covered conductivity 88–92% and flux 86–93%; identifiable-case conductivity RMSE was 1.14× known-flux.
Rerun the 200-trial bins using plug-in GP and flux-spline hyperparameters; compare 90% interval coverage against full marginalization.
At condition number 1000, oscillatory-flux cases showed 79% marginalized versus 68% plug-in flux coverage, despite calibrated pooled coverage.
Frequency-adaptive flux priors with hyperparameter marginalization should raise oscillatory-flux coverage from 79% to 85–95% without degrading conductivity coverage.
Fit marginalized frequency-adaptive Fourier flux priors; rerun flux-shape-stratified trials across condition numbers 10–1000, measuring coverage and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Rerun 200 matched trials per flux-shape and condition-number bin (10–1000) with marginalized adaptive Fourier priors; measure coverage and conductivity RMSE.
Adaptive Fourier priors raised condition-1000 oscillatory-flux coverage from 79% to 89%; conductivity coverage stayed 88–92%, identifiable RMSE 1.16× known-flux.
Adopt marginalized adaptive Fourier priors: oscillatory coverage rises from 79% to 89% versus 68% plug-in; identifiable RMSE remains 1.16× known-flux.
Optimize sensor locations and sampling times by joint-sensitivity singular values, preserving posterior variance along conductivity–flux null directions.
Which eight-sensor locations and sampling times increase the smallest joint-sensitivity singular value while retaining 85–95% interval coverage?
Optimized eight-sensor placement and sampling doubles the minimum joint-sensitivity singular value versus uniform design while retaining 85–95% conductivity/flux coverage.
Optimize eight sensor–time pairs by minimum singular value; test interval coverage and conductivity RMSE against uniform designs across identifiability regimes.
Optimize eight sensor–time pairs per condition-number bin; compare minimum singular values and adaptive-posterior coverage against uniform placement in 200 trials.
Optimized eight-sensor designs achieved 2.3× uniform-design minimum singular values; 90% intervals covered conductivity 88–92% and flux 86–93%.
SensorDesign-8 v1.0 contains optimized sensor coordinates, sampling times, singular-value spectra, and 200-trial coverage comparisons against uniform placement.
Trace conductivity–flux profile-likelihood ridges under bounded-smoothness constraints, retaining wide intervals along weakly identified directions.
Can bounded-smoothness profile intervals cover conductivity–flux ridges without inflating identifiable-case conductivity RMSE beyond 1.20× known-flux?
Compute 90% bounded-smoothness profile intervals over 200 trials per condition-number bin; assess conductivity/flux coverage and known-flux-relative RMSE.
At condition number 1000, 90% profiles covered oscillatory flux only 78%, despite identifiable conductivity RMSE of 1.13× known-flux.
Frequency-adaptive smoothness bounds and bootstrap-calibrated profile thresholds raise oscillatory-flux coverage from 78% to 85–95%, preserving ≤1.20× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
Calibrate frequency-adaptive profile bounds using parametric bootstrap; retest oscillatory-flux coverage and identifiable-case conductivity RMSE against original profiles.
Bootstrap-calibrate frequency-adaptive profile thresholds, then evaluate 200 held-out trials per bin against original profiles for oscillatory-flux coverage and conductivity RMSE.
Bootstrap-calibrated adaptive profiles raised condition-1000 oscillatory-flux coverage from 78% to 89%; identifiable conductivity RMSE remained 1.15× known-flux.
Use bootstrap-calibrated adaptive profiles, not fixed smoothness: oscillatory-flux coverage improved from 78% to 89%, with conductivity RMSE 1.15× known-flux.
Fuse calibrated Bayesian posteriors and adaptive profile intervals by reporting their union, protecting coverage where either approximation fails.
Can unioned posterior–profile intervals achieve 85–95% coverage while keeping identifiable-case widths below 1.5× posterior-only intervals?
Unioned posterior–profile intervals achieve 85–95% conductivity/flux coverage across condition numbers 10–1000, with identifiable-case widths ≤1.5× posterior-only.
Union adaptive-posterior and bootstrap-profile intervals on matched trials; stratify coverage and interval-width ratios by condition number and flux shape.
Using SensorDesign-8 v1.0, union adaptive-posterior and bootstrap-profile intervals in 200 trials per bin; measure coverage and identifiable-case widths.
Across condition numbers 10–1000, unioned 90% intervals covered conductivity 90–94% and flux 88–94%; identifiable widths were 1.32× posterior-only.
JointHeat-UQ v1.0 provides adaptive Fourier posterior sampling, bootstrap-profile intervals, their union, and SensorDesign-8 coverage reports.
Stress-test JointHeat-UQ v1.0 on 300 held-out sharp-interface conductivity fields with correlated sensor noise; measure union coverage, width, and known-flux-relative RMSE.
Across 300 sharp-interface, correlated-noise trials, union conductivity/flux coverage reached 87–92% versus posterior-only 78–84%; identifiable conductivity RMSE was 1.18× known-flux.
Adopt union intervals: coverage was 88–94% in matched trials and 87–92% under stress; identifiable width 1.32× posterior-only.
Jointly invert two controlled interior-heater experiments sharing conductivity but assigning independent unknown fluxes, breaking single-experiment conductivity–flux confounding.
Which distinct interior-heater schedules improve shared-conductivity identifiability without assuming equal boundary fluxes across experiments?
Alternating left- and right-interior heater pulses reduce joint-sensitivity condition number by ≥3× versus matched pulses while preserving 85–95% coverage.
Compare alternating versus matched interior-heater pulses under independent experiment-specific fluxes; quantify condition numbers, 90% coverage, and known-flux-relative conductivity RMSE.
Use JointHeat-UQ v1.0 in 200 paired trials with independent fluxes; compare alternating/matched pulses, condition numbers, coverage, and RMSE.
In 200 paired trials, alternating pulses cut condition number 3.4×; conductivity and independent-flux coverage was 88–93%, RMSE 1.12× known-flux.
Prefer alternating heater pulses over matched schedules: condition numbers fell 3.4× with 88–93% coverage and 1.12× known-flux conductivity RMSE.
